headline: Oxford Street Goes Car-Free: London's Historic Shopping Hub Transforms
meta_description: On October 26, London's Oxford Street closes to all vehicles for the first time, creating a pedestrian plaza on nearly a kilometer of the world's busiest shopp…
summary_short: London's iconic Oxford Street officially becomes car-free on October 26, marking the start of a transformation that shoppers and city planners have debated for years.
body:
On October 26, Oxford Street—one of the world's busiest shopping streets—will close to all vehicles for the first time in its history. London Mayor Sadiq Khan announced the closure of the stretch from Orchard Street to Great Portland Street, nearly a kilometer through the heart of the West End, to buses, taxis, bicycles, and cars. This first phase will feature temporary seating and street-level changes while data is collected before permanent decisions are made. Khan described the transformation as turning the nation's high street into a pedestrian plaza alongside cultural events and next-generation workplaces. The full length of Oxford Street remains in play for later phases.

The announcement comes after years of competing proposals across multiple mayoral administrations. Westminster City Council, which governs the area, has consistently resisted the plan and continues to raise objections, particularly about traffic displacement onto smaller nearby residential and commercial streets. Council deputy leader Tim Barnes called the timeline rushed and questioned whether a full environmental impact assessment was completed. Transport for London and the Oxford Street Development Corporation are managing safety measures and rerouting logistics for the transition.

Historically, pedestrianization works. Copenhagen removed cars from its main shopping street, Strøget, in 1962—retailers predicted lost business, but foot traffic increased instead. New York's Times Square pedestrianization in 2009 and recent car-reduction efforts in Madrid and Oslo have all shown similar results: improved foot traffic and air quality. The real question for Oxford Street isn't whether pedestrianization works in principle, but whether the benefits to the main street justify the adjustment costs for surrounding areas. With 300,000 daily visitors, the next few months of data collection will determine whether London's vision becomes permanent.
quick_facts: Closure begins October 26, 2026 on nearly 1 kilometer of street
Mayor Sadiq Khan announced the transformation after years of delays
First phase uses temporary fixtures to collect data
Copenhagen's similar move in 1962 increased foot traffic
